resolutions.rationale: The footer status link must point at the new brand's own status page. flowpilot.example is a reserved-TLD host that can never resolve to a real company, so inventing it under synthetic-allowed carries no risk of misdirecting a visitor to someone else's service.
A social profile for the pilot brand. Invented and recorded as synthetic; the source destination pointed at the real company's account and could not survive a rebrand.
As above: the source's own code-host organisation cannot be carried onto another brand's footer.
As above.

The source pointed at a specific App Store listing id. A pilot brand has no store listing, and inventing a numeric store id would name a slot that a real listing could occupy; the brand's own download page is the honest destination.
Same reasoning as the iOS link.

The source linked a third party's blog post ABOUT the source product. The equivalent for FlowPilot is FlowPilot's own changelog entry; keeping the third-party post would tell a visitor that another company announced this product.

NOT invented and NOT rebranded: this is a public third-party PROTOCOL SPECIFICATION, not a source-brand destination. Linking a public spec asserts no fact about FlowPilot, so the correct decision is to carry it forward verbatim as derived-copy. Marking it synthetic would falsely claim the engine invented a destination it did not.

The customer story is rewritten as a fictional pilot customer (Northwind Logistics), so its 'company website' link must point at that fictional company on a reserved TLD. Leaving the real customer's domain would present a real business as a FlowPilot customer.
A trust-portal destination for the pilot brand. The source pointed at the real company's trust portal, which cannot survive a rebrand.
Same portal as the SOC 2 request link; both requests are served from one trust portal, which is why the two slots share a destination.
